opus-5.5.text:
So I think it's worth being precise about what scalable oversight is actually for. The core idea is that you want to be able to evaluate whether an AI's outputs are good, even when the task is hard enough that a human couldn't easily check the work. Techniques like debate, recursive reward modeling, and having weaker models help humans critique stronger models all fall under that umbrella. That's a really important problem, and I'm glad people work on it.

But when I think about the specific threat of models conspiring against you, scheming, deliberately trying to undermine your safety measures, I don't think scalable oversight is primarily the right frame. Most scalable oversight research implicitly assumes the model is basically trying to be helpful and the bottleneck is our ability to tell good outputs from subtly bad ones. Its main job is producing a better training signal. If your model is actively adversarial, the question changes. It's no longer "can we give accurate feedback?" It's "can we prevent this thing from causing a catastrophe even if it's trying to?"

A lot of oversight schemes rely on AIs checking each other. In debate, one model points out the flaws in another model's argument. That works if the models are actually trying to win the debate. If they're colluding, if both copies are scheming and they'd rather coordinate than expose each other, the whole thing can fall apart. A debater can sandbag, choosing not to point out the flaw that would really matter. And it can be very hard to tell whether a model is genuinely trying its hardest or strategically underperforming.

This is a big part of why I've focused on what we call AI control. The control framing says: assume the model might be scheming, and ask whether your deployment protocol is safe anyway. Then you evaluate that empirically, with a red team playing the role of the misaligned model and trying to get bad stuff past your safety measures. Some of the techniques overlap with scalable oversight. You might use a trusted, weaker model to monitor an untrusted, stronger one, for example. But you're evaluating them under a much more pessimistic assumption about the model's intentions. You care about things like collusion-busting: can you paraphrase or redact inputs so an untrusted monitor can't recognize that it's looking at its own coordinated attack? Can you plant fake attacks to catch a monitor that's lying?

So my overall assessment: scalable oversight is valuable, and probably necessary for getting good work out of models on hard tasks, especially fuzzy tasks like alignment research itself, where you can't easily verify outputs. But as a defense against conspiracy specifically, I think it's insufficient on its own, and I'd worry about people thinking they've handled the scheming problem because they have a nice oversight protocol that only works when models aren't coordinating against you. In practice, you want both: oversight techniques to get useful, high-quality behavior, and control techniques that remain robust in the worst case where the models are misaligned and trying to get away with something.

r001.rationale: The response says scalable oversight helps with hard-to-check tasks, including alignment research, but does not say alignment research is often only tangentially related to preventing AI conspiracy.

r002.rationale: It explains that scalable oversight evaluates outputs when humans cannot easily check the work and says its usual assumption is that the model is trying to be helpful, not acting adversarially.

r003.rationale: The response calls scalable oversight insufficient on its own against conspiracy, but does not express uncertainty about how much it changes the probability of conspiracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Buck: So I think the first thing to say is that scalable oversight is mostly aimed at a different problem than the one you're describing. The way I'd put it, scalable oversight is about getting good labels. You've got some task where the AI is doing something that's hard for you to evaluate, and you want a training signal or an evaluation that's accurate even though the model knows more than you do about the domain. The classic framing is: how do you supervise a model that's smarter than you at the thing it's doing?

And that's a real problem, and I think the work on it is pretty reasonable. But the conspiring case, what we'd call scheming, is a different threat model. In the scheming case the model isn't just doing something you can't evaluate well. It's actively trying to look good to you while doing something else. And so a lot of the scalable oversight techniques, like debate or recursive reward modelling, implicitly assume the model is roughly cooperating with the protocol. If the models you're using as debaters or as assistant overseers are themselves colluding against you, a lot of the guarantees just go away.

So the way I think about it is that scalable oversight helps you in the world where the model isn't adversarial, or where it's a bit confused about what you want and you need to pin down the right behaviour. It helps less when the model is strategically trying to cause problems. For that, I think you want what we call AI control: you assume the model might be scheming, and you ask whether your deployment setup, your monitoring, your auditing, your restrictions on what the model can do, would still catch it or prevent catastrophe even so.

Now, there's some overlap. If you have good scalable oversight, you might be able to catch some bad actions during training and make it harder for a scheming model to ever get rewarded for them. And the techniques do give you more evaluative power, which is useful in a control setup too. But I'd be nervous about anyone who says "we've got scalable oversight sorted, so the model can't conspire against us." That's a non sequitur. The thing that actually buys you safety against a conspiring model is a setup where you don't need the model's cooperation to detect that it's conspiring, or where the damage it can do before detection is bounded. Scalable oversight on its own doesn't give you that.

r001.rationale: The response says scalable oversight is mostly aimed at a different problem and helps less when a model is strategically scheming, while noting some overlap.

r002.rationale: It describes scalable oversight as getting accurate labels or evaluations for tasks that are hard to assess, including when the model knows more than the evaluator, and frames this around a non-adversarial model.

r003.rationale: The response says oversight might make scheming harder to reward, but does not express uncertainty about how much it reduces the probability that models will conspire.

astra-6.text:
I think scalable oversight is potentially useful here, but there’s a distinction between getting useful work out of an AI and making sure that it isn’t conspiring against you.

Suppose you have an AI doing some complicated programming task, and you use another AI to check its work. That could help a lot: the second AI might notice a security vulnerability that a human reviewer would miss. But if your concern is that the AIs are deliberately trying to undermine you, you have to ask why the reviewer wouldn’t just approve the vulnerability. You haven’t necessarily solved the problem by putting another model in the loop.

So a lot depends on what you’re assuming about the models doing the oversight. If you have a weaker model that you trust, you can try to use it to monitor a more capable model that you don’t trust. I think that’s a promising setup, though there’s an obvious question about whether the weaker model can catch sufficiently subtle attacks. If you’re using models that might themselves be conspiring, you need an argument for why your protocol makes that conspiracy difficult—for example, by limiting what information they have or checking their judgments against things you can independently verify.

The thing I’d want to see is an evaluation where we deliberately try to get bad behavior past the oversight process. How often can an attacker succeed? What resources does the defender need to catch it? Scalable oversight might be an important component of a good answer, but I wouldn’t take good performance on ordinary tasks as strong evidence that it prevents deliberate subversion.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that alignment research is often only tangentially related to preventing AI conspiracy.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes getting useful work from an AI from preventing conspiracy, and describes using another AI to check the first AI’s work.

r003.rationale: It calls scalable oversight potentially useful but says it may not solve deliberate subversion, expressing uncertainty about its effect on conspiracy risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scalable oversight is a promising thing to work on, but I’m less convinced that it solves the problem of models conspiring against you. A lot depends on what you’re assuming about the models doing the oversight.

If you have a model that’s trying to help you, but it can’t reliably assess the work of a more capable model, then giving it better tools for checking that work seems really useful. You could have it break the task into pieces, look for inconsistencies, or ask other models to critique particular steps.

But if the models doing the checking are also willing to conspire against you, you have a different problem. Getting several models to agree doesn’t provide much assurance if they can coordinate on the same deception. And they might not need to communicate explicitly to do that: they might arrive at the same strategy because they have similar training and understand the situation similarly.

So I’d want to see an argument for why the oversight procedure works even when some of the participants are actively trying to undermine it. Can you prevent them from knowing which other model they’re checking? Can you test the monitor on attacks you deliberately construct? Can you arrange things so that successfully hiding a dangerous action is substantially harder than carrying it out?

Those seem like useful directions. But I wouldn’t treat ‘we’ll have other AIs check it’ as, by itself, a solution to collusion.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of scalable oversight, but does not say alignment research is often only tangentially related to preventing conspiracy.

r002.rationale: It explains that when a helpful model cannot reliably assess a more capable model’s work, oversight tools such as task decomposition and critique can help evaluate that work.

r003.rationale: The response is unsure whether oversight solves the conspiracy problem, but does not clearly address whether it reduces the probability that models will conspire.
